title: The gendered organization of exploitation: sex trafficking and masculinity
abstract: Human trafficking is commonly explained through structural inequality, organized crime, coercion and victim vulnerability. While these perspectives explain why exploitation occurs, they tell us considerably less about how perpetrators come to regard exploitation as morally compatible with their own identities and relationships. Drawing on prison ethnography and twenty-four in-depth interviews with men convicted of sex trafficking offences in Romania and Moldova, this article argues that exploitation became morally practicable not because perpetrators abandoned morality but because they differentially allocated its obligations. It develops gendered hierarchical positioning as the relational mechanism through which perpetrators classified themselves and others into unequal gendered positions that distributed care, protection, trust, authority and violence unevenly across social relationships. These acts of positioning simultaneously organized recruitment, intimate relationships and exploitation while enabling perpetrators to construct themselves as providers, protectors, entrepreneurs and comparatively respectable men. By explaining how gendered classification transformed moral differentiation into legitimate conduct, the article offers a new sociological account of how exploitation is organized, sustained and rendered morally acceptable.
